title: Age-related differences in dental caries prevalence and DMFT components among male school students in Najran, Saudi Arabia: a cross-sectional study.
byline: Elamin E, Hyderah K, Daa Khan S, et al.
html: Dental caries remains a significant public health concern during the transition from childhood to adulthood. This study aimed to assess the prevalence and severity of dental caries among male students at the University City Educational Complex in Najran, Saudi Arabia, and to provide a baseline description of oral health in this study population. This cross-sectional study included 586 male students aged 11-18 years, divided into four age groups: 11-12 years (n = 202), 13-14 years (n = 112), 15-16 years (n = 152), and 17-18 years (n = 120). The prevalence of tooth decay was assessed using the Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth Index (DMFT). Of the 586 students examined, 447 had dental caries, and 139 were caries-free. We compared caries prevalence across age groups using the chi-square test with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Population DMFT scores, including zero scores for caries-free participants, were compared using Welch's one-way ANOVA and Games-Howell post hoc tests. Kruskal-Wallis tests were performed as non-parametric sensitivity analyses. The overall prevalence of dental caries was 76.3%. Age-specific prevalence ranged from 67.3% in the 11-12-year group, 78.6% in the 13-14-year group, 78.3% in the 15-16-year group, and 86.7% in the 17-18-year group. Among all 586 participants, the mean DMFT score was lowest in the 11-12-year group (0.78 ± 0.65) and highest in the 17-18-year group (2.93 ± 2.48). Mean DMFT differed significantly across age groups, Welch's F(3, 225.15) = 55.70, p < 0.001. The Kruskal-Wallis sensitivity analysis confirmed this overall difference, H(3) = 94.71, p < 0.001. The Decayed and Missing components differed significantly across age groups, whereas the difference in the Filled component was not robust in the sensitivity analysis. Older age groups had a higher prevalence of dental caries and higher population mean DMFT scores than the youngest group. Untreated decay accounted for most of the DMFT burden, while Filled scores remained low. These cross-sectional findings support strengthening school-based preventive measures and access to timely restorative care during adolescence.
